scenes.text: Your brain can catch your own name in a noisy room, even when you aren't listening.
Psychologists call it the cocktail party effect.
Scientist Colin Cherry named the cocktail party problem in nineteen fifty three.
Early research was driven by air traffic controllers, hearing many pilots' voices mixed over one loudspeaker.
Cherry played a different message into each ear, and people repeated only one of them out loud.
Studies found people remember very little from the ignored ear.
But they did notice when the ignored voice changed pitch or switched gender.
And some even caught their own name in the ignored ear.
Scientists think the brain doesn't fully block the background, it weakens it and keeps listening for what matters.
Babies as young as five months can already pick out their own name.
This trick works best when you hear with both ears.
People with only one working ear tend to be much more distracted by background noise.
The ability seems to peak in young adulthood.
Older adults often find it harder to follow one conversation in a crowd.
Has your name ever jumped out at you from across a noisy room?

title: Why you hear your name in a noisy room 👂
caption: It's called the cocktail party effect: your brain tunes out background voices but still listens for important things, like your own name.
